lesson_title: Flat Beats Nothing, On Edge Beats Flat
hook_text: Same ruler, same steel. Flat, it sags under coins. On edge, it holds a textbook. Here is why beams are shaped like letters.
clip_script: When a beam bends, the top and bottom do all the work and the middle line does nothing. So depth is strength: stand the ruler on edge and it is four times stiffer. Now take that further. The metal in the middle is wasted, so thin it to a web and pile it into a top and bottom flange. That is the I-beam, nearly as strong at a third of the weight. The L, angle iron, is for corners, frames and gates. The T is half an I, for where one face must be flat. Tubes spread the metal evenly all round, so they are best for squashing and twisting: scaffolding, bikes, pylons. Rule: name the force, match the shape, check the fit. And every kilogram of steel you do not need was never mined or smelted. Shape is free strength, and free strength is less harm.
visual_style: Ruler flips from flat to on edge over two books; a solid rectangle morphs into an I with the idle middle fading; letters I, L, T and O line up as cross-sections with force arrows; a scale tips as a solid bar outweighs an I-beam.
pacing: Ruler demo, the neutral axis, the I-beam reveal, three letters, the selection rule.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and find the I, L and T sections on the nearest building site or gate.
